newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Pakistan hopes new road will pay its way.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pakistan hopes new road will pay its way.

text.p: Pakistan plans to open its first toll-paying motorway linking Islamabad and Lahore by the end of 1997, but industry analysts have questioned whether the tolls will raise the anticipated revenue.

Part of a motorway network planned by Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, the six-lane 333-km (208-mile) road between the Pakistani capital and the capital of Punjab province will cost more than 33 billion rupees ($831 million).

South Korea's Daewoo Corp, the main contractor, provided $654 million in supplier credits for the project, which Sharif sees as a first step towards a badly needed modernisation and expansion of Pakistan's decaying national road network.

Tolls were expected to raise two billion rupees ($49.8 million) in the first year of operation in 1998, but some officials of the state-owned National Highway Authority (NHA) privately say receipts may not reach half the targeted figure.
Enamul Haq, secretary at the Communication Ministry, told Reuters recently that most of the work on the road had been done, though some bridges and fencing still had to be completed.
"Our endeavour is to complete the road before the end of the year and open it to the public," he said.
BUT WILL THEY USE IT?

The NHA, supervising the project, has estimated that 9,000 to 12,000 vehicles a day will use the road. At present, 16,000 vehicles a day set out from Islamabad towards Lahore on the old road, while 29,000 each day leave Lahore heading in the opposite direction.

But the motorway route will cover an additional 80 km (50 miles) and critics say the extra distance -- and the toll -- may deter cost-conscious motorists and drivers of ramshackle trucks and buses from using the new road.
"We will know how many vehicles will use the motorway when it opens," said an NHA official, who asked not to be named.
He said the toll, to be adjusted yearly, had tentatively been set at 0.10 rupees per km for cars, one rupee for minibuses, 1.25 for buses, 2.5 for trucks and 3.0 for trailers.
At present, the only multi-lane road in Pakistan's 228,206 km (142,628 mile) network is a two-lane highway between the southern port of Karachi and the northwestern city of Peshawar.
Sharif, an industrialist who initiated the Islamabad-Lahore project during his previous 1991-93 government, believes the new artery will have a huge economic and social impact.

"You will notice the rapid industrialisation when this motorway is opened to traffic," he has said. "Whether you look towards the north or south, the benefits accruing out of the motorway will be beyond imagination."
PLENTY OF PROJECTS, NOT MUCH MONEY
Pakistan expects to begin work this year on a six-lane Peshawar-Islamabad highway for about 22 billion rupees ($543 million), which Haq said could be built in two to three years.
Sharif says his government also plans a highway between Lahore and Faisalabad, a major textile producing centre, and is considering a new Karachi-Peshawar link along the Indus River.
The Indus highway, estimated to cost 20 billion rupees, would reduce the road distance between Karachi and Peshawar by 400 km (250 miles).
"Ultimately, we had planned to establish links with Central Asian states with a series of high-speed roadways," Sharif said.
"The intention is to have motorways all over the country and not confined to one or two regions," Haq said. "But our problem at this time is financial cost."

To overcome its lack of cash, Pakistan wants international firms to build roads on a build own transfer (BOT) basis under which they would recover their investment through tolls and later transfer the roads to the goverment.
"We hope we will be able to get a good response," Haq said.
AFGHAN WAR BLOCKS PAKISTAN'S CENTRAL ASIAN DREAM
Pakistan has long dreamed of becoming a trade conduit for Central Asia, though war in Afghanistan has blocked progress.

"Central Asian trade is definitely an important consideration," Haq said. "The network of motorways will become a high-yielding proposition once the gateway opens after peace comes to that region and traffic starts from there."
"Once this opportunity becomes available there will be a spectacular change in economic terms as far as Pakistan is concerned and these motorways will play a critical role."
However, there are few signs that the long-running conflict in impoverished Afghanistan, which lies between Pakistan and the former Soviet republics, is coming to an end.
